findings.title: The general nonstationary spectral characterization is false
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2001__accepted__v2-genton01a__I01 — The general nonstationary spectral characterization is false
findings.markdown:
**Exact location:** PDF page10 (printed308), Section4, Equation(19) and its introducing paragraph. The analogous local-stationary spectral display begins on PDF page9 (printed307).

**Affected central claim and assumptions.** The paper asserts that a nonstationary kernel on R^d is positive definite if and only if it is a double integral of cos(omega1^T x - omega2^T z) against a positive bounded symmetric measure F. It presents this as the spectral characterization of its most general kernel class and a way to design many new nonstationary kernels. No simultaneous inversion symmetry assumption is imposed on kernels. Spectral representation and spectral kernel design are explicit contributions in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

**Demonstrable error.** Every function represented by the displayed cosine integral necessarily obeys

    K(-x,-z) = K(x,z),

because cosine is even. This holds for any F for which the integral exists, including signed or positive-definite bimeasures; it is not a terminology issue about “positive.” But the bounded, smooth one-dimensional kernel

    g(x) = exp(-(x-1)^2),
    K(x,z) = g(x) g(z)

is positive semidefinite by the paper's own Equation(6), since every finite quadratic form equals (sum_i lambda_i g(x_i))^2. It has K(1,1)=1 and K(-1,-1)=exp(-8). It therefore has no representation of the stated cosine form. This refutes the necessary direction even for a simple rank-one Gaussian-shaped kernel; discontinuity, unboundedness and pathological nonharmonizability play no role.

Under the ordinary nonnegative-measure assumption that the paper states, the sufficient direction also fails. Give mass1/4 to each frequency pair(0,1),(1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0). This F is finite, nonnegative, symmetric under exchange of the two frequencies, and symmetric under simultaneous reversal. Equation(19) then gives

    K(x,z) = (cos(x) + cos(z))/2.

For inputs0 and pi, its Gram matrix is diag(1,-1); the second diagonal is a negative variance. Thus the purported spectral recipe can return a function that is not a kernel. The correct spectral PSD condition is a quadratic condition on a bimeasure, not scalar nonnegativity of its mass. Primary definitions inspected for this distinction appear in [Kom Samo's thesis](https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~sjrob/Theses/yvesLaurentKomSamo_thesis.pdf), Definitions7.5–7.6, PDFpp192–193, and [Generalized Spectral Kernels](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.02236), Theorem6. The cosine parity counterexample is independent of that distinction.

 The script verifies both counterexamples symbolically. A further check uses the bounded rank-one kernel sin(x)sin(z): any nonnegative F would have total mass K(0,0)=0 and hence be zero, contradicting K(pi/2,pi/2)=1.

**Why it matters.** Equation(19) is the central general spectral characterization, not an isolated evaluation error. It excludes elementary smooth bounded valid kernels and its stated sufficient assumptions admit negative variances. Repair requires changing the spectral representation to accommodate complex/sine contributions, imposing the essential spectral PSD condition, and stating the actual representation domain. Those changes replace the advertised general nonstationary design theorem. The error directly defeats the paper's stated method for characterizing and constructing the most general class of kernels.

**Discovery:** Structural invariance analysis of the cosine integrand, followed by exact finite-atom integration and a check of primary spectral-bimeasure definitions.  
**Verification:** Original rendered PDF rechecked; exact symbolic reproduction; independent verification by the parent reviewer of the parity obstruction. All14 pages and the remaining claims were reviewed after identifying the candidate.  
**Confidence:** High. The leading counterexample is an exact two-value contradiction and does not depend on how “positive” is interpreted.
findings.html:
Exact location:

PDF page10 (printed308), Section4, Equation(19) and its introducing paragraph. The analogous local-stationary spectral display begins on PDF page9 (printed307).

Affected central claim and assumptions.

The paper asserts that a nonstationary kernel on \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is positive definite if and only if it is a double integral of \(\cos(\omega_1^T x-\omega_2^T z)\) against a positive bounded symmetric measure F. It presents this as the spectral characterization of its most general kernel class and a way to design many new nonstationary kernels. No simultaneous inversion symmetry assumption is imposed on kernels. Spectral representation and spectral kernel design are explicit contributions in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

Every function represented by the displayed cosine integral necessarily obeys

\[K(-x,-z)=K(x,z),\]

because cosine is even. This holds for any F for which the integral exists, including signed or positive-definite bimeasures; it is not a terminology issue about “positive.” But the bounded, smooth one-dimensional kernel

\[\begin{aligned}g(x)&=\exp\!\left(-(x-1)^2\right),\\K(x,z)&=g(x)\,g(z)\end{aligned}\]

is positive semidefinite by the paper's own Equation(6), since every finite quadratic form equals \(\left(\sum_i\lambda_i g(x_i)\right)^2\). It has \(K(1,1)=1\) and \(K(-1,-1)=\exp(-8)\). Under the ordinary nonnegative-measure assumption that the paper states, the sufficient direction also fails. Give mass1/4 to each frequency pair(0,1),(1,0),(0,-1),(-1,0). This F is finite, nonnegative, symmetric under exchange of the two frequencies, and symmetric under simultaneous reversal. Equation(19) then gives

\[K(x,z)=\frac{\cos(x)+\cos(z)}2.\]

For inputs0 and \(\pi\), its Gram matrix is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\); the second diagonal is a negative variance. Thus the purported spectral recipe can return a function that is not a kernel. The correct spectral PSD condition is a quadratic condition on a bimeasure, not scalar nonnegativity of its mass. Primary definitions inspected for this distinction appear in Kom Samo's thesis, Definitions7.5–7.6, PDFpp192–193, and Generalized Spectral Kernels, Theorem6. The cosine parity counterexample is independent of that distinction.

The script verifies both counterexamples symbolically. A further check uses the bounded rank-one kernel \(\sin(x)\sin(z)\): any nonnegative F would have total mass \(K(0,0)=0\) and hence be zero, contradicting \(K(\pi/2,\pi/2)=1\).

Equation(19) is the central general spectral characterization, not an isolated evaluation error. It excludes elementary smooth bounded valid kernels and its stated sufficient assumptions admit negative variances. Repair requires changing the spectral representation to accommodate complex/sine contributions, imposing the essential spectral PSD condition, and stating the actual representation domain. Those changes replace the advertised general nonstationary design theorem. The error directly defeats the paper's stated method for characterizing and constructing the most general class of kernels.

Discovery:

Structural invariance analysis of the cosine integrand, followed by exact finite-atom integration and a check of primary spectral-bimeasure definitions.

Verification:

Original rendered PDF rechecked; exact symbolic reproduction; independent verification by the parent reviewer of the parity obstruction. All14 pages and the remaining claims were reviewed after identifying the candidate.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: The formula imposes a symmetry that valid kernels need not have. Conversely, the stated nonnegative measure condition can produce a negative variance.
sections.markdown: The formula imposes a symmetry that valid kernels need not have. Conversely, the stated nonnegative measure condition can produce a negative variance.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
Every kernel produced by the formula has simultaneous sign-reversal symmetry. The valid rank-one kernel below does not:

\[ K(x,z)=e^{-(x-1)^2-(z-1)^2},\qquad K(1,1)=1\neq e^{-8}=K(-1,-1) \]

A separate permitted four-point spectral measure produces the following expression, whose diagonal is negative at \(\pi\):

\[ K(x,z)=\frac{\cos x+\cos z}{2},\qquad K(\pi,\pi)=-1 \]

findings.title: The proposed quality measure rewards arbitrarily poor coverage
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2001__accepted__v2-jonyer01a-01 — The proposed quality measure rewards arbitrarily poor coverage
findings.markdown:
**Exact locations.** PDF p15 / printed p33, Section4.6.1, first coverage requirement and end of Section4.6.2 introduction; PDF p16 / printed p34, displayed Quality and Coverage definitions; PDF p17 / printed p35, claim that all desired properties are measured and the worked numerical example. The same example's0.836 score is used in the principal comparison in Section5.4.1, PDF p21 / printed p39. The metric supports the further quantitative comparisons in PDF pp20–22 / printed pp38–40 and is expressly identified as a major contribution on PDF p23 / printed p41.

**Affected claim.** Section4.6.1 requires greatest coverage with the smallest possible number of clusters, large cluster descriptions and little overlap. Section4.6.2 claims its measure rewards these properties. However, it defines

\[
Q(L,G)=\frac{D(\operatorname{root}L)}{\operatorname{Coverage}(L,G)},\qquad
\operatorname{Coverage}(L,G)=\frac{\left|\bigcup_{C\in L}\bigcup_i C_i\right|}{|G|},
\]

where graph size counts vertices plus edges. Coverage is the represented fraction, not the uncovered fraction. Larger quality is expressly preferable. With every other criterion fixed, this formula strictly prefers **less** represented input.

**Exact same-input counterexample.** Let each of four labeled directed motifs A,B,C,D consist of two vertices and one edge. For motif T, label its vertices T0,T1 and its edge Te. The alphabets are disjoint and equal in length; the four motifs are related by bijective label renaming. Form one fixed input graph G from100 disjoint copies each of A and B and2 copies each of C and D. Thus G has408vertices and204edges, for size612. Disconnected graphs are expressly permitted in Section3.1, PDF p4 / printed p22.

Compare two valid classification hierarchies, each an administrative root and exactly two leaf clusters:

* L_common contains clusters A and B, including **all100 matches** of each.
* L_rare contains clusters C and D, including **all2 matches** of each.

No matches of a selected definition are discarded. Both hierarchies have the same topology, number of clusters, description sizes and zero overlap. Each cross-cluster instance pair has edit distance3, achieved by relabeling the two vertices and the edge. Dividing by size3 gives1. Averaging10000 identical comparisons for L_common or4 for L_rare therefore gives the same root diversity1. Leaves contribute0, as in the paper's worked example. Independently, singleton-vertex motifs give the same result with unambiguous edit distance1. More generally, any alternative label-symmetric edit convention gives the same positive diversity in both hierarchies and the same ranking ratio.

| Hierarchy | Covered items | Coverage | Diversity | Published quality |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| L_common |600|50/51|1|51/50=1.02|
| L_rare |12|1/51|1|51|

The measure favors the hierarchy covering1.96% of the input over the otherwise equivalent hierarchy covering98.04%, by a factor50. For M copies of each common motif and R copies of each rare motif, the preference factor is M/R, which is unbounded. This is an internal failure of the paper's explicitly stated coverage property, without relying on subjective cluster labels or an outside definition of good clustering.

The root is administrative and does not itself count as the entire input graph. This follows the paper's convention: its own root-containing Figure8 hierarchy has coverage104/111, rather than1.

**The division is used in the reported evaluation.** The prose on PDF p16 once says multiplied, but the displayed equation and full worked computation on PDF p17 divide. The disclosed numbers give

\[
D=\frac{11.2+14.4+12.0}{48}=\frac{47}{60},\quad
C=\frac{104}{111},\quad
D/C=\frac{1739}{2080}=0.83605769\ldots.
\]

That0.836 value is reused as the Figure8 result in Section5.4.1, PDF p21. Multiplication instead gives D*C=1222/1665=0.73393393…, a different reported result and the opposite ordering in the exact counterexample. Thus the evidence does not support dismissing this as an isolated typesetting error. The original2001 evaluation program was not recovered; a later2011 author-distributed source archive does not contain the quality measure and cannot establish historical implementation details.

**Why it matters.** The metric is one of the paper's declared major contributions and supplies its quantitative argument for objective clustering quality and superiority over Cobweb. Its central defining coverage property fails arbitrarily badly while every other stated preference is held fixed. Repair requires a changed evaluation criterion and renewed quantitative validation; editing an explanatory sentence cannot preserve the current metric's behavior. The clustering construction itself is not disproved. The evidence also does **not** establish that every published animal or web ranking reverses: the necessary score components and original evaluation files are unavailable. It establishes that the proposed general quality measure fails its claimed purpose and consequently cannot supply the asserted objective validation.

**Discovery.** Traced the desired properties in Section4.6.1 into the denominator in Section4.6.2, then checked the rendered formula, coverage definition, worked arithmetic and reuse in the main comparison. Continued through all25pages, all figures/table, conclusions and references; no appendix is present.

**Verification.** Independently generated the same input graph and both complete occurrence lists, evaluated all quantities with exact rational arithmetic, and checked structural and singleton variants. The script also reconstructs the actual0.836 score from the paper's disclosed components. Reproduce with:

Evidence: counterexample script, exact results, input graph, and original page renders p15, p16, p17, p21, p23.

**Confidence: high.** The inverse coverage preference and unbounded ratio follow exactly from the printed definitions, with all relevant assumptions matched. The repeated numerical result demonstrates that division is consequential to the reported evaluation. Historical implementation and benchmark-ranking consequences are expressly bounded above.

findings.title: Pointwise deletion stability does not imply the claimed empirical bound
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v2-bousquet02a-01 — Pointwise deletion stability does not imply the claimed empirical bound
findings.markdown:
**Location:** PDF page 8 (printed page 506), Theorem 11, first bound and proof. The relevant pointwise stability is Definition 4 on PDF page 5 (printed page 503); the sample-size convention appears on PDF page 6 (printed page 504).

**Affected claim:** The empirical generalization bound

\[
R\leq R_{\rm emp}+\sqrt{\frac{M^2+12Mm\beta_2}{2m\delta}}
\]

uses only pointwise hypothesis deletion stability \(\beta_2\).

**Error and reproducible counterexample:** Let \(X=\{0,\ldots,9\}\), all true labels be \(+1\), and let the input distribution be uniform. Fix the following deterministic learner, for every sample length: \(A_S(x)=-1\) exactly when the number of sample inputs different from \(x\) equals 4; otherwise it predicts \(+1\). Use the bounded 0–1 loss, so \(M=1\).

Deleting a training example at \(x_i\) does not change the number of sample inputs different from \(x_i\). Therefore pointwise deletion stability is exactly zero at every sample size, including samples with repeated inputs. The learner is symmetric and measurable. Its hypothesis deletion stability admits the nonincreasing bound \(\min\{1,5/n\}\), so the paper's stability-rate convention does not exclude it.

At sample size \(m=4\), the learner predicts every training input correctly and every unseen input incorrectly. Thus \(R_{\rm emp}=0\) and \(R\geq 0.6\) for every sample. Setting \(\delta=1/2\), the theorem instead gives \(R\leq 0.5\), allegedly with probability at least \(1/2\). Exhaustive enumeration of all \(10^4\) ordered samples confirms that **every sample violates the bound**. The mean true risk is exactly \(6561/10000\).

**Discovery:** Traced which point is used in the deletion-versus-replacement comparison in Definition 4, Lemma 9, and Theorem 11.

**Verification:** The exhaustive finite check includes all repetitions. For completeness, at any sample size \(n\), let \(q=9/10\), the probability that an independent training input differs from a fixed test input. Deleting the selected training input changes the test loss exactly when that input differs from the test input and the other \(n-1\) inputs contain either 3 or 4 inputs different from it. Thus the exact hypothesis stability is

\[
\beta_1(n)=q\left[\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(n-1,q)=3\}+\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(n-1,q)=4\}\right].
\]

The binomial identity \(nq\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(n-1,q)=k\}=(k+1)\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(n,q)=k+1\}\) gives

\[
n\beta_1(n)=4\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(n,q)=4\}
 +5\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(n,q)=5\}\leq5.
\]

Because the two binomial events are disjoint, the displayed weighted sum is at most 5. Hence \(\beta_1(n)\leq5/n\), as well as \(\beta_1(n)\leq1\), establishing the stated nonincreasing upper envelope.

The original rendered theorem and proof were checked. The proof incorrectly bounds a test-point comparison by training-point stability \(\beta_2\); the available bound is \(\beta_1\).

**Why it matters:** A principal generalization theorem for the paper's weaker stability notion supplies a false certificate on every possible sample. Repair requires a different stability quantity or a stronger definition, rather than a constant adjustment to the stated bound.

**Confidence:** High. The finite learner satisfies the stated assumptions, its stability is exact, and every sample is checked.

sections.title: Claim in the paper

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
The audit uses ten equally likely inputs, all labeled +1, and four training examples. Its learner always predicts training labels correctly and has zero pointwise deletion instability, but misclassifies at least six of the ten inputs.

\[ R_{\mathrm{emp}}=0,\quad \beta_2=0,\quad R\geq0.6>0.5=\text{claimed upper bound} \]

findings.title: The SVR risk certificate omits target uncertainty
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v2-bousquet02a-02 — The SVR risk certificate omits target uncertainty
findings.markdown:
**Location:** PDF page 18 (printed page 516), Example 1, its loss bound and final generalization bound. The assumptions and epsilon-insensitive loss begin on PDF page 17 (printed page 515).

**Affected claim:** The displayed bounded, bias-free SVM regression bound

\[
R\leq R_{\rm emp}+\frac{\kappa^2}{\lambda m}
 +\left(\frac{2\kappa^2}{\lambda}
 +\kappa\sqrt{\frac B\lambda}\right)
 \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2m}}.
\]

**Error and reproducible counterexample:** Let the input space contain one point, with nonzero kernel \(k(x,x)=1\). Its RKHS consists of constant functions \(c\), with squared norm \(c^2\). Set \(B=\kappa=1\), \(m=1\), \(\lambda=10000\), \(\epsilon=1/4\), and \(\delta=0.1\). Let labels 0 and 1 each have probability \(1/2\).

The specified SVR objective is

\[
\max\{0,|c-y|-1/4\}+10000c^2.
\]

Its unique minimizers are \(c=0\) for training label 0 and \(c=1/20000\) for training label 1. Both outputs lie in \([0,1]\). Its exact uniform deletion stability at \(m=1\) is \(1/20000\), matching the example's stability estimate.

On the event that the training label is 0, which has probability \(1/2\), the empirical loss is zero and the true risk is

\[
R=(0+3/4)/2=3/8=0.375.
\]

The displayed risk upper bound is instead **0.011044426734075671**. Thus its claimed 90% confidence certificate fails with probability 50%.

The substituted loss bound \(M\leq\kappa\sqrt{B/\lambda}=0.01\) is false: at prediction 0 and target 1, the loss is 0.75. The target-scale term remains positive as regularization forces predictions toward zero.

**Discovery:** Tested the claimed loss bound in the large-regularization limit, then constructed a scalar SVR problem with exactly solvable minimizers.

**Verification:** Convexity and the derivative on the active loss segment establish both minimizers. The two equiprobable samples were enumerated and their risks, empirical losses, stability, and claimed bounds computed independently. The original rendered Example 1 and parameter ranges were checked. The example uses positive epsilon, a nonzero kernel, and \(\delta<e^{-1}\).

**Why it matters:** SVM regression generalization bounds are prominently advertised in the abstract and conclusions. The stated certificate is false even when its stability estimate is exact. Its entire penalty tends to zero as \(\lambda\) increases, although label uncertainty persists, so no universal multiplicative constant repairs the claimed regularization dependence.

**Confidence:** High. There are only two scalar convex optimization cases; the counterexample does not depend on unbounded predictions or an omitted clipping convention.

Run the evidence with:

Exact results, full-paper coverage, screened candidates, and original-render references are preserved in unpublished audit files, `review_notes.txt`, and the review JSON. The related least-squares boundedness candidate is retained as evidence but is not counted as a third finding.

findings.title: Fixed sample indices do not remove data-dependent shattering complexity
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2002__accepted__v2-cannon02a-01 — Fixed sample indices do not remove data-dependent shattering complexity
findings.markdown:
**Location:** Section 4.2, PDF pages 9–10 (printed pages 343–344): the singleton-class paragraph and the fixed center-index / fixed-radius cells of both shatter-coefficient tables. Definition 1 appears on PDF page 4 (printed page 338). Section 6, PDF page 22 (printed page 356), reiterates the claimed complexity reduction.

**Affected claim and assumptions:** The paper claims that predetermining the sample indices of the sphere centers, and fixing their radii, gives shatter coefficient 1. The allowed number of centers is \(q\leq n\). These are predetermined **sample indices**, not coordinate locations: the original headings say “Center Index Dependency,” and Section 6 explicitly says fixing these indices can violate sample permutation symmetry.

**Error:** Definition 1 counts dichotomies over the union of classes generated by **all** training subsamples of the evaluation points. A class containing one classifier after a particular sample is observed can therefore have a large data-dependent shatter coefficient. The singleton argument and table cells omit this union.

**Exact counterexample and consequence:** Fix \(q=100\) before observing the data and evaluate at \(n=q=100\). Let \(X=[0,1]\), with ordinary Euclidean distance and uniform input distribution. All labels are 1. Predetermine center indices \(1,\ldots,100\) and the positive radius \(r=10^{-6}\) for every center. The resulting class contains the single classifier

\[
h_S(x)=\mathbf 1\left\{\min_{1\leq i\leq100}|x-x_i|\leq10^{-6}\right\}.
\]

The centers are distinct almost surely, so \(q\leq n_1\) holds. The classifier is jointly Borel measurable. Every training input is covered, so empirical classification error is zero. The union of balls has measure at most

\[
2nr=\frac1{5000}.
\]

Thus its true classification error satisfies

\[
e(h_S)\geq\frac{4999}{5000}=0.9998
\]

with probability 1. Applying the paper’s supplied coefficient \(S_{100/200}=1\) in Theorem 3, with \(m=200\) and \(\epsilon=1/2\), would instead assert

\[
\Pr\{|e(h_S)-\widehat e(h_S)|>1/2\}
\leq 2e^{2\epsilon}e^{-n\epsilon^2/2}
=2e^{-11.5}\approx0.0000202602.
\]

The actual probability is 1. The generic theorem with the **correct** shatter coefficient is not contradicted; the paper supplies an invalid complexity bound for its advertised application.

**Independent count:** Choose the 200 evaluation points \(x_j=j/201\). Their separation exceeds \(2r\). A classifier trained on any 100-point subsample covers exactly those 100 evaluation points. Hence Definition 1 gives

\[
S_{100/200}\geq\binom{200}{100}
=90548514656103281165404177077484163874504589675413336841320,
\]

rather than 1. Complementing the classifier to form the loss indicators preserves this count. Exhaustive small instances give \(2,6,20,70,252,924\) dichotomies for \(n=1,\ldots,6\), matching \(\binom{2n}{n}\).

**Discovery:** Compared the paper’s combined-subsample definition with the realized-singleton argument, then tested the explicitly permitted case \(q=n\).

**Verification:** Rechecked the original table headings, the \(q\leq n\) restriction, the sample-index interpretation and Section 6’s symmetry statement. The counting argument is exact; the risk calculation follows from the total interval length and needs no missing experimental artifact.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying computational/performance tradeoffs for these classifier families is a principal contribution. The supplied bound gives a sharp false error certificate to a trivial-computation memorizer whose true error is almost maximal. Correcting the coefficient from 1 to an exponentially large quantity at \(q=n\) materially changes the advertised tradeoff. This is not a constant adjustment or a harmless table typo. The separate variable-center consistency theorem uses a different, correctly larger coefficient and is not claimed false.

**Confidence:** High. Every parameter is fixed before sampling, the radius is positive, the data and learner satisfy the measurability assumptions, and the lower bound on true error holds for every relevant sample.

Run the evidence with:

Full-paper checks, screened candidates, results and rendered-original references are preserved in unpublished audit files and the review JSON.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
Use 100 uniform points in [0,1], all with label 1, and radius 10⁻⁶ around each training point. The classifier memorizes the sample but covers almost none of the input interval.

\[ R_{\mathrm{emp}}=0,\qquad R\geq0.9998 \]

The supplied coefficient makes Theorem 3 bound the probability of a large error by about 0.0000203, although that error occurs with probability 1. Across subsamples of 200 distinct points, there are binomial(200,100) label patterns.
